transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-25 09:42 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Ellis (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Maya Rios (Head of ML, Cobalt), Tom Hsu (CTO), Evan Park (Platform Eng), Lena Ortiz (Product)

Summary (auto):
Cobalt is evaluating Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment for a conversational product with cost sensitivity. Primary success criteria: keep per-conversation cost under $0.03 while meeting 400ms p50 latency for 1k concurrent users. Discussed batching, K V cache patterns, quantization tradeoffs, and pilot scope. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share cost model and pilot options, customer to provide sample prompts and traffic profile, schedule benchmark call.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone can you hear me all good?
[00:06] Maya: yeah good, thanks Jordan, sorry a bit overbooked this morning.
[00:10] Jordan: no worries, we'll run about 40 minutes. quick context: i'm Jordan AE on Redwood, priya is our systems engineer, she's gonna walk through technical levers. want to start with high level goals - Maya over to you.
[00:24] Maya: sure. so we're building a shopping assistant for mobile and web. typical session is multi-turn, average turn length about 120 tokens, sometimes up to 400 for longer explanations. goal is to keep user-facing latency snappy and control cost — finance gave us a per-conversation ceiling of around three cents. we have compliance on PII redaction but not strict residency needs yet. timeline is Q4 pilot.
[00:46] Tom: and from infra side we run on GCP but open to hybrid; if private is required we can do VPC peering, probably not air gap. main concerns: burst traffic during flash sales, and cost predictability.
[00:59] Priya: thanks, that's helpful. quick clarifying question: when you say per-conversation do you mean end-to-end full session token sum or per request?
[01:06] Maya: per session, all prompts plus model replies, so aggregate token cost. average session is 3 requests.
[01:13] Priya: good, ok. so three requests at ~120 tokens each -> ~360 tokens/session typical.
[01:18] Jordan: from a pricing perspective we have hosted per-token, and for dedicated/reserved capacity we can do committed throughput pricing that lowers unit cost but adds reservation. private deployments add platform fees + infra. we'll sketch three pilot options today.
[01:29] [00:30] Maya: awesome. can you ballpark hosted per-token? we've seen numbers from other vendors but need apples-to-apples.
[01:36] Jordan: rough hosted numbers: for the open-model family we typically quote X cents per 1k prompt tokens and Y cents per 1k output tokens, but i will put exact up-to-date lines in the sheet. ballpark for the model class you're thinking (mix of 7-13B-ish) is about $0.6 to $1.2 per 1k total tokens on hosted, dependent on throughput and if you enable streaming.
[01:56] Tom: that sounds higher than our expectations. we calculated a target of $0.03/session at 360 tokens — that implies about $83 per 1k tokens? wait that math seems off.
[02:08] Jordan: yeah the math differs since you may be counting only prompt tokens — we should align. if you budget 360 tokens * sessions per month — let's walk through sample compute.
[02:16] [01:15] Evan: small note, our current traffic estimate is 250k sessions / month at launch tapering to 1M in six months.
[02:23] Jordan: ok so at 250k sessions * 360 tokens = 90M tokens / month. at $1 per 1k tokens that's $90k. at $0.5 per 1k that's $45k. so to get to $0.03 per session (250k sessions) you'd need overall spend ~7.5k which implies ~$0.083 per 1k tokens — so yes that's an aggressive target.
[02:45] Maya: hmm, right we may need to tune prompts and reuse context caching to hit an effective token reduction. can you talk about batching and K V cache? we currently reuse session state server-side but we send context every request.
[02:57] Priya: sure. two main levers: batching (combine concurrent requests to improve GPU utilization) and KV (key-value) cache or prefix cache that avoids re-sending large system prompt + history on each request. Redwood's runtime supports automatic prefix caching and token-level KV cache so you can keep prompt overhead low. small caveat: caching works best when you have repeat prefixes — for multi-turn shopping flows it's often effective for system prompts and product description templates.
[03:25] [02:30] Evan: is KV cache the same as keeping the whole conversation in memory? what about security of cached tokens?
[03:31] Priya: it's the attention key/value cache we keep on the server for the model (not persisted plaintext prompts). for hosted we encrypt at rest, and we can configure eviction. for private we can give you KMS controls. the transcript generator sometimes calls it K V cache so apologies for the lingo.
[03:44] Tom: ok, so that reduces prompt tokens sent but not model-generated tokens, right?
[03:49] Priya: exactly — caching mainly reduces input token overhead. for model outputs you'd need shorter replies or reranking. also batch sizes help: if you have bursts, continuous batching improves throughput and lowers per-token GPU cost, but may add a few ms to tail latency.
[04:03] [03:15] Maya: latency is important — our p50 target is 400ms. can you achieve that with batching enabled?
[04:09] Priya: yes. with tuned batching and smaller sequence lengths we've seen p50 in the 200-350ms range for 7–13B models on dedicated pools. hosted SLAs vary, but we can set up dedicated capacity if latency is a firm requirement.
[04:21] Lena: question on quantization — can we quantize models to lower cost and what's the quality hit?
[04:27] Priya: quantization (4-bit/8-bit) helps a lot on throughput and memory; 4-bit may have minor quality regression for some instruction-heavy samples. Redwood Optimize can recommend which quant profile to use based on your eval set. we'll run a quick A/B on your prompts in the pilot.
[04:40] [03:45] Maya: you mentioned dedicated reserved capacity — what's the commitment and how much does unit cost drop?
[04:46] Jordan: typical dedicated offers: small reserved pool (equivalent to X GPUs) monthly commit which lowers per-token by 20–40% depending on utilization. there's also burst capacity for traffic spikes. the tradeoff is you'd be paying a base monthly seat. I'll include two commitment tiers in the options.
[05:02] Tom: if we go private VPC, does Redwood still handle control plane? and how does pricing change?
[05:09] Jordan: for private we run a control plane in our managed network and the inference plane in your VPC; pricing has platform fee plus infra pass-through. it tends to be higher up-front but gives you tighter security and control and can be cost-effective at very large scale because you manage instance selection.
[05:24] [04:15] Evan: what about fallback strategies? if a dedicated pool is saturated during a sale can you failover to hosted or a smaller cheaper model?
[05:32] Priya: yes smart routing can fallback to compatible model variants or other regions, it's part of our serving runtime. fallback to a smaller quantized variant is common.
[05:40] Maya: do you have examples from other retail customers on per-conversation numbers after caching and batching?
[05:46] Jordan: generally for shopping chat we see effective token reductions of 20–40% with prefix caching and template reuse, and batching can lower token cost by another 10–30% depending on concurrency shape. so a 360-token nominal session might behave like 230–280 effective tokens for billing. of course results vary by prompt hygiene.
[06:08] [05:15] Maya: that helps. one more: how do you measure quality regressions after quantization? we can't accept higher drop in NPS.
[06:15] Priya: we tie evals to your prompts and metrics (exact match, BLEU-ish, and human review samples). Redwood Optimize will flag regressions beyond thresholds and we can tune quant profiles per endpoint.
[06:27] Lena: are audit logs and SSO included? our security team needs SAML + full request logs for audits.
[06:33] Jordan: SAML SSO, RBAC, and audit logs are available on dedicated and private. hosted has standard audit trails; for enterprise retention we offer add-on longer log retention. we'll send the security packet.
[06:45] [06:00] Tom: ok, finances — can you show a worked example for our 250k sessions month with hosted vs small dedicated vs private?
[06:53] Jordan: yes i'll prepare three worked scenarios: 1) hosted w/ no reservation, 2) dedicated small pool with 1-month commit, 3) private eval with platform fee. each will show per-1k token assumptions, caching factor, batching factor, and final monthly spend + per-session effective cost.
[07:10] Evan: for the dedicated scenario, what's the minimum pool size? and how elastic is it?
[07:16] Priya: minimum is often a single node equivalent; we recommend starting with a small reserved pool and enabling autoscale/burst for peaks. elasticity depends on model and infra; autoscaling can add/remove nodes with minutes of lead time.
[07:27] [07:30] Maya: what will you need from us to run the pilot?
[07:31] Jordan: sample prompts, typical concurrency profile, SLOs, and a small eval set. priya will need infra contacts for the benchmarking call.
[07:39] Priya: and if you want private eval we'll need network IPs for peering and credentials for your KMS if you plan to bring keys.
[07:46] [08:00] Tom: question — i've seen other vendors talk about "token-slicing" or "request multiplexing" are those different from batching?
[07:55] Priya: token-slicing is a way to break long sequences—more common for very long context to stream through—whereas request multiplexing/batching is combining independent requests to fill a GPU batch. both can reduce cost but they have different latency/complexity tradeoffs. we can recommend approaches based on your prompt distribution.
[08:10] Maya: regarding ROI, our product team is ok with a slight latency bump if it substantially reduces cost. what are acceptable p95 tradeoffs?
[08:17] Priya: p95 will increase more than p50 with batching. in our experience if you target p50 300–400ms p95 can be 800–1,200ms depending on burst shape. can tune policies to preserve p95 at cost of higher unit price.
[08:34] [09:15] Jordan: quick objection we've seen a few customers worry about vendor lock with private deployments — how easy is it to migrate models?
[09:21] Priya: we support model export and standard model formats; migration has operational work but we keep it transparent. for private you run the inference plane, so switching vendors would mean re-deploying your runtime, but model artifacts are standard.
[09:33] Lena: will you share a Jupyter with quick A/B on our prompts?
[09:36] Jordan: yes we'll include a sandbox notebook in the pilot packet.
[09:41] [10:00] Maya: ok sounds good. can we try a micro-pilot: 2 weeks, hosted with KV caching enabled + a small dedicated pool for peak windows — that way we can compare metrics quickly.
[09:46] Priya: that's a reasonable approach. micro-pilot parameters: 2 weeks, we enable prefix cache on hosted endpoints, and we provision a small dedicated pool for scheduled peak windows. we'll collect p50/p95, token counts, and cost.
[09:58] Jordan: i'll include an estimated budget for the micro-pilot in the email.
[10:02] [11:30] Tom: last question from me — are there any hidden charges we should watch out for? network egress for private deployments?
[10:10] Jordan: network egress is passed through on private, and for hosted we include basic egress but large regional transfer could add. also long-term KV retention and extended log retention are add-ons. we'll call those out clearly.
[10:22] Maya: perfect. thanks everyone.
[10:26] Jordan: quick recap of next steps: Jordan sends cost model + three pilot scenarios by Friday 2026-08-27; Priya drafts bench plan; Maya shares sample prompts and traffic shape. schedule bench call for the week of Sept 7. any other items?
[10:40] Maya: nothing else from me. thanks.
[10:42] Jordan: thanks all, we'll follow up with the packet.
[10:45] [END]
